Accessibility

The behavior the components are supposed to have, and where it comes from. Most of it is already in the platform — a native <dialog> traps focus on its own, a <details> is searchable, a radio group handles its own arrow keys. The work is knowing which parts the platform does not supply and writing those by hand.

The overlay contract

Everything that covers the page owes the same four things. The table says which of them the browser provides and which this kit has to add — the difference is entirely whether the thing is a native <dialog>.

Obligation dialog drawer / sheet popover / menu
Tab stays inside Platform By hand Not modal
The page behind is unreachable Platform inert Not modal
Escape closes it Platform By hand By hand
Focus returns to the trigger Platform By hand By hand

This is the argument for showModal() over a div with a high z-index: four obligations met for free, none of which can then drift. A drawer cannot be a dialog — it is a layout element that happens to be modal on small screens — so it gets the same four applied explicitly.

Try each one with the keyboard

Tab leaves this, on purpose. A popover is not modal, so trapping focus in one would strand anybody who opened it by accident.

With any of the first three open, Tab will not reach this page. Escape closes the innermost one and puts focus back on the button that opened it.

Focus trapping

Confining Tab is the visible half. The half that gets forgotten is inert, which removes everything behind the overlay from the accessibility tree as well as the tab order — without it a screen reader can still read, and a pointer can still click, a page the sighted reader believes is covered.

What inert does

/* Not focusable, not clickable, not read aloud,
   not found by in-page search. One attribute. */
<main inert>…</main>

What it replaces

/* Hides from assistive tech but stays clickable
   and still takes Tab. Not a substitute. */
<main aria-hidden="true">…</main>

UI.trapFocus(element) applies both, and keeps a stack so a sheet opened over a drawer unwinds in the right order. UI.releaseFocus(element) undoes it and hands focus back — but only if focus is still inside what is closing, so a deliberate move elsewhere in the meantime is not overridden. 

/* Everything beside the surface goes inert, except the scrim, which
   has to stay clickable, and the toast region, which has to stay
   announceable. */
UI.trapFocus(mySurface);

/* …later */
UI.releaseFocus(mySurface);
warning

A trap with nothing to focus is a cage

If a surface holds no focusable element, focus has to land somewhere or the keyboard is stuck on a page it cannot see. The surface itself is given tabindex="-1" and takes focus, which is also what makes its label get read on open.

Roving tabindex

A composite widget is one tab stop, not forty-two. Tab moves to the widget; the arrow keys move inside it. Every grid and list in this kit follows it, which is why tabbing through a page with a calendar on it does not take a minute.

One tab stop

How it works

Exactly one day carries tabindex="0"; every other carries -1. An arrow key moves the zero and calls focus() on the new holder. Leaving and returning with Tab comes back to where you were, not to the first of the month.

The same shape drives comboboxes, except that focus never moves at all — the input keeps it and aria-activedescendant points at the highlighted row. That is the pattern to use whenever typing must continue while a selection moves.

Forced colors

In Windows High Contrast and other forced-color modes the browser replaces every color the stylesheet set with one from a small system palette. A design language that carries meaning in a background tint loses that meaning entirely — and this one carries almost everything that way. Separating planes by fill rather than by outline is the whole idea, and forced colors is precisely the mode in which the idea stops working, so nearly every surface and control has to be given an edge back here.

visibility_off

What disappears

  • Elevation, which is a step along the fill ladder and nothing else.
  • Hover, focus and pressed states, which are translucent fills over that ladder.
  • Status color on tags, chips, dots and alerts.
  • Progress bars and meters, which are a colored fill in a track.
  • Fields, chips and the neutral button, which have a fill and no border.
check_circle

What replaces it

  • A real 1px solid CanvasText border wherever elevation was the only edge.
  • Highlight and HighlightText for anything selected.
  • GrayText for anything disabled.
  • forced-color-adjust: none on the few fills that must survive.
  • An outline on the focus ring, whose token color is ignored.
@media (forced-colors: active) {
  /* Depth is a fill, and fills do not survive, so every plane needs an edge. */
  .card, .popover, .menu, .dialog, .widget { border: 1px solid CanvasText; }

  /* Same for every control that gave up its border to get one. */
  .input, .search, .choice-chip, .button-outlined { border: 1px solid CanvasText; }

  /* A state layer is a translucent fill, so selection must be redrawn. */
  .listbox-option[aria-selected="true"],
  .calendar-day.is-selected {
    background: Highlight;
    color: HighlightText;
    forced-color-adjust: none;
  }
}
info

Testing it

In Chrome and Edge: DevTools → Rendering → "Emulate CSS media feature forced-colors". In Firefox, about:config → browser.display.document_color_use → 2. Emulation gets you most of the way; the real thing on Windows catches the rest.

Right to left

Set dir="rtl" on <html> and the whole kit mirrors. Most of that is free: the layout is built from logical properties — padding-inline, inset-inline-start, border-inline-end — which follow the document's writing mode without being told to. Try it on any page in this kit:

Currently left to right.

The text stays English, so this shows the layout mirroring rather than a translation — which is exactly what needs checking.

Three things do not come free, and they are the whole of section 21 of the stylesheet.

open_in_full

Transforms

Always physical

translateX(-101%) slides a drawer off the left edge whatever the direction, because a transform has no notion of a writing mode. Every sliding surface — drawer, side sheet — needs its own mirrored rule. Absolutely positioned chrome is the same story wherever it had to name a physical side.
arrow_forward

Icons that point

Some, not all

An arrow meaning "onward" points right in English and left in Arabic, so it is flipped. An icon that depicts an object must not be: a mirrored clock, printer or magnifier reads as a mistake rather than a translation. Only the directional set is flipped, and .icon-directional opts one in by hand.
code

Islands of LTR

Not everything mirrors

Code, file paths, version strings and phone numbers are not translated and must not be reordered by the bidi algorithm. They get direction: ltr so they read as written, inside an otherwise right-to-left page.

The keyboard mirrors too

This is the part that is easy to miss. CSS flips the layout, but → is a physical key and always will be: in a mirrored list the next item is to the left. Every horizontal arrow handler in the kit asks which way the text runs before deciding what "next" means — tabs, the carousel, the calendar grid, the one-time code, the toolbar and the board all go through one helper, UI.isRTL(el). Vertical keys never change, and neither does a vertical toolbar.

The direction is read from the element rather than from <html>, because a single component inside a right-to-left page can be marked dir="ltr" — a code block or a phone number — and its arrow keys should follow its direction, not the page's.

What to check when you mirror

  • check_circle The drawer and the side sheet slide in from the correct edge.
  • check_circle Breadcrumb separators, pagination and “next” arrows point the right way.
  • check_circle Clocks, printers, magnifiers and other depicted objects are not mirrored.
  • check_circle Code blocks, paths and numbers still read left to right.
  • check_circle Arrow keys move in reading order in tabs, calendars and the board.
  • check_circle The native select chevron sits on the leading edge, with the padding to match.
  • check_circle Nothing is clipped at the start edge — a stray physical margin-left is the usual cause.

Reduced motion

prefers-reduced-motion is a request about vestibular safety, not a taste. Movement goes; the state change stays, because a thing that appears instantly is still a thing that appeared.

In the stylesheet

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: .01ms !important;
    transition-duration: .01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

In the script

/* Press feedback is an instant change of fill, so
   there is no travel to shorten and nothing to
   suppress: it is already correct under reduced
   motion. The gestures that do move — the drawer,
   a dialog, a toast — are the ones guarded. */
if (prefersReducedMotion()) return;

.01ms rather than 0, so a transitionend handler still fires and nothing that waits on one hangs for ever.

Live regions

Anything that changes without the reader doing it has to be announced, and the choice between polite and assertive is the whole decision: assertive interrupts whatever is being read, which for anything short of a failure is rude.

ThingRolePolitenessWhy
ToaststatuspoliteConfirms something the reader just did; it can wait a sentence.
Form error on submitalertassertiveNothing proceeds until it is dealt with.
Result count after filteringstatuspoliteOtherwise a filter appears to do nothing.
Chat loglogpoliteAnnounces arrivals without taking focus off the composer.
Reorder announcementstatuspoliteA keyboard move is otherwise completely silent.
Upload progressprogressbaroffA percentage read aloud every tick is unusable.

The region has to be in the document before the text goes into it. Inserting an already-populated live region announces nothing in most screen readers — which is the single most common reason an announcement silently fails.

Labelling

An icon button with no label announces as "button". That is the most common failure in any component kit, and it is also the easiest to find — every icon-only control in this kit carries aria-label.

Wrong

<button class="button button-icon">
  <span class="icon">delete</span>
</button>

<!-- announces: "button" -->

Right

<button class="button button-icon"
        aria-label="Delete this draft">
  <span class="icon">delete</span>
</button>

<!-- announces: "Delete this draft, button" -->

The rest of the rules

  • label The label says what happens, not what it looks like "Delete this draft", never "Trash icon".
  • group Repeated controls need distinguishing Twelve "Edit" buttons in a table are twelve identical announcements. "Edit replicas for production" is one.
  • hide_image Decorative icons are hidden, not labeled An icon beside its own text label is read twice unless it carries aria-hidden="true".
  • star A set of shapes gets one label, not five A reported rating is role="img" with aria-label="4.3 out of 5"; five separate star icons announce as noise.
  • visibility Visible text beats an invisible label Prefer aria-labelledby pointing at text on screen, so what is read matches what is seen — which is also what voice control needs.

Keyboard map

Every interactive component in the kit, and what the keyboard does in it. If a component is not on this list it is a plain button, link or field and behaves as the platform does.

ComponentKeys
Combobox ↓↑ move · HomeEnd ends · Enter choose · Esc close · Tab commit and leave
Calendar ←→ day · ↑↓ week · PgUpPgDn month · HomeEnd week ends · Enter choose
Tag field Enter or , add · Backspace arm, then remove
Number stepper ↑↓ step (native to the field)
One-time code ←→ move · Backspace clear and step back · Ctrl+V fills every box
Rating ←→ change (native to the radio group)
Reorder Enter pick up · ↑↓ move · Enter drop · Esc cancel
Inline edit Enter commit · Esc revert · blur commits
Popover Esc close and return focus · Tab leaves, by design
Menu Esc close · any item closes it
Tabs ←→ move between tabs
Dialog Esc close · Tab cycles inside (both native)
Carousel ←→ previous and next slide
Sortable table Enter on a header toggles the sort

What to check

In rough order of how often each one is broken. None of it needs a tool beyond the browser you already have open.

  1. 1 Unplug the mouse and use the page Everything reachable, nothing trapped, the focus ring always visible and always where you expect.
  2. 2 Tab through with every overlay open The place traps break is the second overlay, not the first.
  3. 3 Zoom the browser to 200% Nothing clipped, nothing scrolling sideways, no fixed element covering the content.
  4. 4 Read the headings in order One h1, no skipped levels, and the outline alone should describe the page.
  5. 5 Turn the color off Forced-color emulation, then a grayscale filter. Anything that only differed by hue has now vanished.
  6. 6 Turn motion off Every state change still happens; nothing waits on an animation that no longer plays.
  7. 7 Listen to one flow end to end VoiceOver, NVDA or Narrator, on the one journey that matters most. Ten minutes here finds more than any automated scan.

A sheet is modal too

So it gets the same four obligations as a dialog, applied by hand. Tab will not leave this, and Escape puts focus back on the button that opened it.

The platform did all of this

Tab cycles inside, Escape closes, the page behind is unreachable and focus returns to the button you pressed — none of which is scripted here. showModal() provides all four.

The only thing added is where focus lands: data-autofocus puts it on the safe option rather than on whatever happens to come first.
